summary: Router Advertisements are sent by IPv6 routers to announce their presence and settings. Sending them too often can drain the battery of hosts that must wake up to process each one. This best current practice recommends operational choices to avoid that impact.

plainLanguage.summary: If someone keeps ringing the doorbell every few seconds, you can never rest. This says routers should not announce themselves so often that sleeping gadgets run out of battery.

questions: how often should ipv6 router advertisements be sent
should routers reply to router solicitation with unicast
subtitle: Why sending IPv6 Router Advertisements too often drains batteries, and what networks and devices should do about it.

tldr.problem: Frequent Router Advertisement messages wake sleeping battery-powered hosts, hurting battery life and sometimes making hosts ignore RAs or all IPv6 packets while asleep.
tldr.mechanism: Networks should answer Router Solicitations with unicast RAs where appropriate and avoid frequent multicast RAs, while hosts that process unicast packets in sleep must also process multicast RAs and may rate-limit identical ones.
tldr.outcome: No protocol changes are needed; the RFC gives operational practice (BCP 202) using behavior already allowed by RFC 4861.

facts.label: RA power budget
facts.value: No more than 0.1 mA (2% of idle)

today: RFC 7772 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 202) and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It adds no protocol changes and relies on behavior already allowed by RFC 4861.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: IPv6 hosts learn routing information from Router Advertisement (RA) messages defined in RFC 4861. If those messages are sent too frequently, they can severely hurt power consumption on battery-powered hosts. This RFC recommends operational practices to avoid that.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers shout "I am here and this is how to reach the internet!" Shouting too often tires out the gadgets listening.

sections.title: The Two Problem Scenarios
sections.content:
The first scenario is solicited multicast RAs on large networks. Every time a device joins, all devices on the link receive a multicast RA. If devices keep joining and leaving on a large enough network, everyone receives solicited RAs at the maximum rate allowed by Section 6.2.6 of RFC 4861, which is one every 3 seconds.

The second is frequent periodic RAs, sometimes sent every few seconds. Operators may do this to limit customer impact of renumbering events, which in some large residential networks happen relatively often. Some hosts ignore RAs or even all IPv6 packets in sleep mode, so networks send RAs often to avoid leaving devices with non-functional IPv6 configurations. This has a severe impact on battery life.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a classroom where every time a new kid walks in, the teacher announces the rules to everyone again. If kids keep coming and going, nobody gets any peace.

sections.title: Consequences and the Right Frequency
sections.content:
The observed effects include bad battery life on otherwise normal hosts, hosts that drop all RAs in power-saving mode (losing connectivity), and hosts that drop all IPv6 packets in power-saving mode. It gets worse: some administrators respond to RA-dropping devices by sending RAs even more often, which causes even more aggressive filtering.

The right frequency depends on how constrained the devices are. Laptop-class devices likely see no noticeable impact even with RAs every few seconds. Tablets, phones and watches feel it more. The RFC's example figures are about 5 mA with the main processor asleep and about 200 mA for 250 ms on receiving a packet, so one RA costs roughly 0.014 mAh.

To keep RA reception to 2% of idle power, the budget is no more than 0.1 mA, or approximately 7 RAs per hour. Because multicast may be lost or rate-limited while asleep, lifetimes such as the default router lifetime might reasonably be 5 to 10 times the RA period, roughly 45 to 90 minutes. Sensor networks and similar non-general-purpose networks may have tighter needs and even longer intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: A big laptop barely notices a tap on the shoulder. A tiny watch with a small battery notices every single one, and they add up.

sections.title: Recommendations for Networks
sections.content:
Router manufacturers SHOULD let administrators configure routers to answer Router Solicitations with unicast RAs when the solicitation's source address is not the unspecified address and it contains a valid Source Link-Layer Address option. Administrators of networks serving large numbers (tens or hundreds) of battery-powered devices SHOULD enable this.

Such networks SHOULD NOT send multicast RAs too frequently unless the RA's information has substantially changed. To get hosts to notice a change quickly, they MAY send frequent RAs for a limited time (for example not more than one minute) right after a configuration change.

No protocol changes are required: unicast replies to solicitations are already allowed by Section 6.2.6 of RFC 4861, and RA intervals are already configurable over a wide range.
sections.plainLanguage: When one new kid arrives, tell only that kid the rules instead of announcing them to the whole class. Only make a big announcement when something really changes.

sections.title: Recommendations for Devices
sections.content:
Staying connected over IPv6 requires receiving periodic multicast RAs. So hosts that process unicast packets sent while they are asleep MUST also process multicast RAs sent while asleep. Battery-powered hosts MAY rate-limit identical RAs that arrive too frequently.

Battery-powered devices that do not intend to keep IPv6 connectivity while asleep SHOULD either disconnect from the network, abandoning all IPv6 configuration there, or run Detecting Network Attachment in IPv6 (DNAv6) procedures from RFC 6059 on waking.
sections.plainLanguage: A gadget that listens while napping must listen to the router's announcements too. If it does not want to listen, it should say goodbye and ask again when it wakes up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Misconfigured or malicious hosts that send rogue Router Advertisements (see RFC 6104) can also severely hurt battery-powered hosts' power consumption if they send many such messages. Any IPv6 network where such hosts are possible should take appropriate countermeasures.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster who keeps ringing the doorbell can drain a sleeping gadget too, so networks should watch out for pranksters.
